w: The Council of Europe has sat here since 1977, when this building replaced the modest 'House of Europe' along the same street. For over two decades it doubled as the Strasbourg seat of the European Parliament, before MEPs moved down the road to the newer Louise Weiss building.
s: Seat of the Council of Europe since 1977
_facts: Seat of the Council of Europe since 1977, replacing the 'House of Europe'
Also served as the Strasbourg seat of the European Parliament 1977-1999

w: Tanners, millers and fishermen once worked this stretch of the Grande Ile, where the Ill splits into a lattice of channels beneath half-timbered houses. Officially the Quartier des Tanneurs, everyone still calls it Petite France - the most photographed corner of Strasbourg's UNESCO-listed old town.
s: Where the Ill splits into a maze of tanners' canals
_facts: Medieval quarter of tanners, millers and fishermen where the Ill river splits into channels
Officially Quartier des Tanneurs; part of the UNESCO World Heritage Grande Ile, listed 1988

w: At 313 kilometres, this was the longest canal in France when it opened in 1853, threading Paris and the north all the way to the Rhine at Strasbourg's port. It was built to stitch Alsace and Lorraine into the rest of the country - decades before the borders around it would move twice more.
s: France's longest canal when it opened in 1853
_facts: 313 km canal linking the Marne to the Rhine at Strasbourg's port
Longest canal in France when it opened in 1853; built to connect Paris/north France to Alsace-Lorraine, the Rhine and Germany

n: Musee d'Art Moderne et Contemporain de Strasbourg
w: One of France's largest museums of its kind, MAMCS holds 18,400 works spanning Impressionism to now, plus an art library, a bookshop, and a roof terrace cafe with views over the Ill. It grew out of a 1973 city collection and only got a purpose-built home in November 1998.
s: 18,400 works of modern art, plus rooftop views
_facts: Founded 1973, opened in its own building November 1998
Holds 18,400 works spanning 1870-present; one of the largest museums of its kind in France; rooftop cafe terrace
_sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strasbourg Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art

n: Bibliotheque Nationale et Universitaire de Strasbourg
w: A public library facing the Palais du Rhin across the Place de la Republique - the old Kaiserplatz, from the years this whole quarter was built as Strasbourg's German Empire showpiece. Its reading rooms have sat in that imperial shadow ever since.
s: Reading rooms facing the old Kaiserplatz
_facts: Public/national academic library on Place de la Republique, formerly Kaiserplatz
Faces the Palais du Rhin

w: Strasbourg's German-built New Town, added to the Grande Ile's UNESCO listing in 2017, fuses Haussmann-style boulevards with Wilhelmine architecture on a scale barely seen even in Germany - most comparable quarters there were flattened by Allied bombing in the Second World War.
s: The Kaiser's new quarter, still standing
_facts: District built under the German Empire; UNESCO-listed in 2017 as an extension of the Grande Ile site
Merges Haussmannian planning with German imperial architecture; best-preserved example of its kind, since comparable German districts were bombed in WWII

w: The former Kaiserpalast dominates the Place de la Republique with a dome built for maximum imperial swagger - a palace designed to put German rule in Strasbourg on full display. The gardens and stables around it are just as much a 19th-century architectural showpiece as the building itself.
s: The Kaiser's palace still guards its old square
_facts: Former Imperial Palace (Kaiserpalast) in the German quarter of Strasbourg, dominating Place de la Republique (former Kaiserplatz) with its dome
Landmark of 19th-century German architecture, with surrounding gardens and stables

w: Built for the Kaiser's garrison, this Gothic Revival church has 19 separate doors - nearly triple the cathedral's seven - so soldiers of every rank up to the Emperor himself could enter without mixing. Its three rose windows borrow their design from the Elisabeth Church in Marburg.
s: 19 doors, built to keep the ranks apart
_facts: Built 1892-1897 for the Lutheran members of the Imperial German garrison; 19 portals versus the cathedral's 7, to accommodate all ranks including the Emperor
Three rose windows modelled on the Elisabeth Church of Marburg; handed to the Protestant Reformed Church in 1919

w: Jean Calvin preached from this small Gothic pulpit in 1538, and Albert Schweitzer played its organ as pastor here from 1900 to 1913 - two very different giants of conscience, three centuries apart. It no longer holds regular parish services, but a charismatic congregation has met here since 1975.
s: Calvin preached here; Schweitzer played the organ
_facts: Jean Calvin led services and preached here in 1538
Albert Schweitzer was pastor 1900-1913 and played the organ; no longer a parish church, used by a charismatic group (Renouveau Saint Nicholas) since 1975

w: The mother house of the Opera national du Rhin has anchored Place Broglie since the 19th century, right in the heart of the Grande Ile. It's been a monument historique since 1921 - one more grand facade on a square that was already Strasbourg's ceremonial front room.
s: Mother house of the Opera national du Rhin
_facts: Main seat and mother house of Opera national du Rhin, on Place Broglie on the Grande Ile
Classified monument historique since 1921

w: A small Art Nouveau hotel particulier tucked onto the Rue Sleidan, one of the quieter architectural gems among the Neustadt's grid of grand German-era townhouses. Listed as a monument historique since 1975, it rewards anyone who looks up while walking through the district.
s: An Art Nouveau townhouse hiding in plain sight
_facts: Small Art Nouveau hotel particulier on Rue Sleidan in the Neustadt
Classified monument historique since 1975

w: Once known as the Hotel Gayot, this Place Broglie mansion has served as the official residence of Strasbourg's military governor, and been a monument historique since 1921. It shares the square with the Opera house - two grand faces on the city's ceremonial heart.
s: Home to Strasbourg's military governor since 1921
_facts: Formerly Hotel Gayot, on Place Broglie on the Grande Ile
Monument historique since 1921; currently the official residence of the military governor of Strasbourg

n: Palais de la Musique et des Congres
w: Home to the Orchestre philharmonique de Strasbourg since 1975, this concert hall and convention centre anchors the Wacken district near the European quarter - proof that Strasbourg's civic ambitions extend well past its medieval core.
s: Home of the Strasbourg Philharmonic since 1975
_facts: Music venue and convention centre in the Wacken district, close to the European quarter
Home of the Orchestre philharmonique de Strasbourg since 1975
_sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palais de la musique et des congres

w: One of the longest-running of Strasbourg's churches, tucked near the railway station on the city's western edge. Lutheran since the Reformation, it's stayed quietly off the tourist trail despite a history and architecture that easily rival the Grande Ile's bigger names.
s: One of Strasbourg's oldest churches, off the trail
_facts: One of the Strasbourg churches with the longest history, near the railway station
Lutheran church since the Reformation

w: The fourth church on this site since the 13th century, rebuilt in near-Jugendstil style after a fire gutted it in 1904, then destroyed again in the Second World War and rebuilt once more. A historic monument since 1898, it has simply refused to stay down.
s: Burned, bombed, and rebuilt - four times over
_facts: Fourth church dedicated to Mary Magdalene on this site since the 13th century
Rebuilt close to Jugendstil style after a fire in 1904; destroyed again in WWII and reconstructed; historic monument by decree of 1898

w: Another Art Nouveau hotel particulier on the Neustadt's Allee de la Robertsau, listed since 1975 - and since 1992, home to the European Audiovisual Observatory, which quietly tracks Europe's film and TV industries from behind its ornate facade.
s: Art Nouveau mansion turned EU film-data office
_facts: Art Nouveau hotel particulier on Allee de la Robertsau in the Neustadt, monument historique since 1975
Seat of the European Audiovisual Observatory since 1992

w: The crypt holds the remains of a fifth-century Roman basilica, and the church above it was founded in 717 by Duke Adalbert of Alsace, who installed his own daughter as its first abbess. Rebuilt Romanesque-Gothic in 1220, it later served as a warehouse, then a theatre, after the Revolution stripped it bare.
s: A Roman crypt under a church founded by a duke
_facts: Crypt contains remains of a 5th-century Roman basilica, on the site of a former Roman fort
Founded 717 by Duke Adalbert of Alsace, who installed his daughter Attala as first abbess; rebuilt Romanesque-Gothic in 1220; used as warehouse then theatre after the Revolution
